label: Neyman–Pearson, MLR and UMP tests — mastery test (unseen)

items.stem: The Neyman–Pearson lemma gives the most powerful test for:
options: a simple null against a simple alternative
a simple null against a composite alternative
a composite null against a composite alternative
items.explanation: The lemma is stated for two completely specified hypotheses. Composite alternatives need monotone likelihood ratio and Karlin–Rubin, and even then only for a one-sided alternative.

items.stem: The size of a test is:
items.explanation: Size is the Type I error rate, computed entirely under the null. Option A is power, option D is β, and option C is also β written the long way.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₁₆ are iid N(μ, 36) with σ² = 36 known. Test H₀: μ = 10 against H₁: μ = 13 at α = 0.05. Give the critical value for x̄.
items.explanation: σ/√n = √36/√16 = 6/4 = 1.5, so the region is x̄ > 10 + 1.645(1.5) = 10 + 2.47 = 12.47. Option D mistakes the alternative for the critical value — the alternative never appears in the cut-off, and option B uses σ² where σ belongs.
items.check: The critical value uses μ₀, σ, n and α only. If the number 13 appears in it, the size condition has been computed under the wrong hypothesis.

items.stem: Continuing the previous setting — n = 16, σ = 6, H₀: μ = 10, H₁: μ = 13, reject when x̄ > 12.47. Give the power of the test.
items.explanation: Power = P(X̄ > 12.47 | μ = 13) = P(Z > (12.47 − 13)/1.5) = P(Z > −0.355) = 0.639. Option C is β = 1 − power, the probability of missing a shift of this size.
items.check: Power must exceed α whenever the alternative differs from the null, and β = 1 − power. An answer of 0.05 means the power was evaluated at μ₀ rather than μ₁.

items.stem: Consider the Neyman–Pearson lemma and what it delivers.
items.explanation: A is true — the lemma is a statement about tests of equal size. B is false: the constant is fixed by the size condition under H₀, so the alternative never enters it. C is true, and it is why the lemma holds in full generality for discrete data. D is true — among size-α tests none has greater power.
statements: The lemma compares tests of the same size α.
The critical value depends on the value of the alternative.
A randomised test may be needed to attain size exactly α.
No size-α test has greater power than the likelihood ratio test.

A.why: Power is only comparable between tests of equal size; otherwise you could buy power with α.

B.why: P(reject | H₀) = α fixes the constant. The alternative sets the direction and the power only.

C.why: Discrete statistics attain only finitely many sizes; randomising on the boundary closes the gap.

D.why: That is precisely the conclusion of the lemma.

items.stem: Monotone likelihood ratio in T means that:
options: the likelihood itself is a monotone function of θ
for every θ₂ > θ₁ the ratio f(x;θ₂)/f(x;θ₁) is a non-decreasing function of T
T is a monotone function of the parameter
the power function is monotone in T
items.explanation: MLR is a condition on the RATIO of two densities, required for every pair of parameter values, and it says the ratio depends on the data only through T and moves one way in T. It is the hypothesis of the Karlin–Rubin theorem.

items.stem: For which testing problem does a UMP test fail to exist in the N(μ, σ²) family with σ² known?
options: H₀: μ ≤ μ₀ against H₁: μ > μ₀
H₀: μ = μ₀ against H₁: μ = μ₁ with μ₁ > μ₀
H₀: μ = μ₀ against H₁: μ ≠ μ₀
H₀: μ ≥ μ₀ against H₁: μ < μ₀
items.explanation: The two-sided alternative is the standard failure. The most powerful test against an alternative above μ₀ rejects in the upper tail and the one against an alternative below rejects in the lower; the two regions are disjoint, so no single test is best against both. The other three are one-sided or simple and all have UMP or MP tests.

items.stem: Consider uniformly most powerful tests.
items.explanation: A is true — this is Karlin–Rubin. B is true: one-parameter exponential families with increasing natural parameter have MLR in the natural statistic. C is false, and it is the headline failure of the topic: two-sided alternatives admit no UMP test. D is true — the unbiasedness restriction eliminates the one-sided candidates and leaves the two-tailed test as UMPU.
statements: MLR in T gives a UMP test for a one-sided alternative.
A one-parameter exponential family has MLR in its natural statistic.
Every testing problem has a UMP test if the family is an exponential family.
For the two-sided normal mean, the UMPU test is the symmetric two-tailed test.

A.why: Karlin–Rubin, which is how a composite one-sided alternative is handled.

B.why: With a strictly increasing natural parameter, which covers the binomial, Poisson, normal mean and exponential.

C.why: Two-sided alternatives have no UMP test even in the nicest families.

D.why: Unbiasedness rules out both one-sided regions; the symmetric two-tailed test is best among what remains.

items.stem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid Bernoulli(p). For testing H₀: p ≤ p₀ against H₁: p > p₀, the UMP test rejects when:
options: ΣXᵢ > c, with c fixed by P(ΣXᵢ > c | p₀) = α
ΣXᵢ < c, with c fixed by P(ΣXᵢ < c | p₀) = α
ΣXᵢ > c, with c fixed by P(ΣXᵢ > c | p₁) = α
items.explanation: The Bernoulli is a one-parameter exponential family with natural parameter log(p/(1−p)), increasing in p, so it has MLR in ΣXᵢ and Karlin–Rubin gives an upper-tail region. The size is evaluated at the boundary p₀, which is where a composite null is worst.
items.check: For a composite null H₀: p ≤ p₀, the size is the supremum over the null — attained at the boundary p₀. Evaluating anywhere else understates it.

items.stem: A test of H₀: μ = 100 against H₁: μ > 100 rejects when x̄ > 104, with σ = 15 and n = 36. Give the size of the test.
items.explanation: σ/√n = 15/6 = 2.5, so the standardised cut-off is (104 − 100)/2.5 = 1.6 and the size is P(Z > 1.6) = 0.0548. Option A is the complement and option C uses a standard error of 1 rather than 2.5.
items.check: Size is an upper-tail probability under H₀, so it should be small. Any answer above 0.5 has the tail the wrong way round.

items.stem: The power function β(θ) of a test evaluated at θ = θ₀ equals:
options: the size α of the test
items.explanation: β(θ) = P(reject | θ), so at the null value it is exactly the Type I error rate. This is the standard consistency check on any power function you derive: if it does not return α at θ₀, the derivation is wrong.

items.stem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid Exponential with mean θ. For H₀: θ = θ₀ against H₁: θ = θ₁ with θ₁ > θ₀, the most powerful test rejects when:
options: Σxᵢ < c, with 2c/θ₀ the lower-α point of χ²(2n)
Σxᵢ > c, with 2c/θ₁ the upper-α point of χ²(2n)
x̄ > c, with c the upper-α point of N(θ₀, θ₀²/n)
Σxᵢ > c, with 2c/θ₀ the upper-α point of χ²(2n)
items.explanation: The ratio is (θ₀/θ₁)ⁿ exp{Σxᵢ(1/θ₀ − 1/θ₁)}, and with θ₁ > θ₀ the coefficient is positive, so the ratio increases with Σxᵢ — reject for large totals. Under H₀, ΣXᵢ is Gamma(n, θ₀), equivalently 2ΣXᵢ/θ₀ is χ²(2n), which is the form the tables take. Option B sizes the test under the alternative.
items.check: Two checks: the direction should agree with intuition (a larger mean makes a larger total plausible), and the constant must be fixed under θ₀.

items.stem: Consider the two error types and how they move.
items.explanation: A is true — at fixed n, moving the cut-off trades one error against the other. B is false: increasing n lowers β at fixed α, which is the whole reason to collect more data. C is true, and is the floor on power. D is true by definition of an unbiased test.
statements: At a fixed sample size, lowering α raises β.
Increasing the sample size raises β at fixed α.
A test's power at the null value equals its size.
A test is unbiased if its power never falls below its size.

A.why: One cut-off, two tails: moving it to shrink one area grows the other.

B.why: The opposite. Larger n narrows both sampling distributions, so β falls with α unchanged.

C.why: β(θ₀) = α by definition of the power function.

D.why: β(θ) ≥ α for every θ in the alternative — which the one-sided tests violate on the far side.

items.stem: A one-sided test of a normal mean has power 0.60 at a particular alternative with n = 25. Roughly what sample size would raise the power to about 0.85 at the same alternative and the same α = 0.05?
items.explanation: Power depends on the alternative through (μ₁−μ₀)√n/σ. For power 0.60 the quantity z_α − (μ₁−μ₀)√n/σ is about −0.253, giving (μ₁−μ₀)/σ ≈ (1.645 + 0.253)/5 = 0.3796. For power 0.85 we need z_α − (μ₁−μ₀)√n/σ = −1.036, i.e. √n ≈ (1.645 + 1.036)/0.3797 = 7.06, so n ≈ 50. The lesson's point stands: power rises with √n, so doubling the sample is nothing like doubling the power.
items.check: Power scales with √n, not n. Doubling the sample does not double the power, and the closer power gets to 1 the more each extra point costs.

items.stem: In testing a discrete parameter, a randomised test is used in order to:
options: increase the power beyond the Neyman–Pearson bound
attain a size exactly equal to α when no ordinary critical region does
avoid having to compute the likelihood ratio
items.explanation: A discrete statistic attains only finitely many tail probabilities, so an exact size of 0.05 is usually unavailable. Rejecting with probability γ on the boundary interpolates between two achievable sizes. It does not change the lemma's bound, and it has nothing to do with unbiasedness.

items.stem: Arrange the steps of applying the Neyman–Pearson lemma in order.
items.explanation: Form the ratio first, then simplify it into an inequality on a statistic — that step tells you which statistic and which direction. Only then fix the constant from the size condition under H₀, and compute power under H₁ last, if the question asks for it.
items: A. Simplify the ratio into an inequality on a statistic
B. Compute the power under H₁
C. Form the likelihood ratio L(θ₁)/L(θ₀)
D. Fix the constant from P(reject | H₀) = α

items.stem: X₁,…,X₉ are iid N(μ, 9) with σ² = 9 known. The test rejects H₀: μ = 0 when |x̄| > 1.96. Give the size of this two-sided test.
items.explanation: σ/√n = 3/3 = 1, so x̄ is standard normal under H₀ and P(|X̄| > 1.96) = 2(0.025) = 0.05. The standard error being exactly 1 is what makes 1.96 the familiar number here.
items.check: A two-sided region takes α/2 in each tail, so the total is 0.05, not 0.025. Option B is one tail only.

items.stem: Consider what happens when a UMP test does not exist.
items.explanation: A is true — the disjointness of the two one-sided regions is the standard argument. B is true: a one-sided test has power below α on the far side, which is exactly what 'biased' means. C is true, and the UMPU test is the two-tailed one. D is false — the likelihood ratio test is always available but is not optimal in general; that is precisely why UMPU is introduced.
statements: No UMP test exists two-sided because the two one-sided optimal regions are disjoint.
The one-sided test is biased against alternatives on the opposite side.
Restricting to unbiased tests yields the symmetric two-tailed test for the normal mean.
The likelihood ratio test is uniformly most powerful whenever a UMP test fails to exist.

A.why: Uniqueness of each MP test forces a UMP test to equal both disjoint regions at once.

B.why: Its power dips below α for alternatives on the far side — the definition of a biased test.

C.why: Unbiasedness removes both one-sided candidates; the two-tailed test is best among the rest.

D.why: The LRT is a general-purpose fallback with good asymptotics, not an optimality result.

items.stem: 'Uniformly' in uniformly most powerful means the test is most powerful:
options: at every value in the alternative, simultaneously
items.explanation: The word quantifies over the alternative. A most powerful test is best against one specified alternative; a uniformly most powerful test is best against all of them at once, which is a far stronger demand and is why such tests often fail to exist.

items.stem: A one-parameter family has MLR in T. For testing H₀: θ ≤ θ₀ against H₁: θ > θ₀ at level α, the size of the Karlin–Rubin test is computed at:
options: θ = θ₁, a value in the alternative
the value of θ minimising the power
any θ in the null, since the size is the same throughout
θ = θ₀, the boundary of the null
items.explanation: For a composite null the size is the supremum of the rejection probability over the whole null. Under MLR the power function is non-decreasing in θ, so that supremum is attained at the boundary θ₀ — which is why the condition is written P(T > c | θ₀) = α. Option C is false precisely because the power function varies across the null.
items.check: A composite null takes its size from its worst case. Evaluating anywhere inside the null understates the true Type I error rate.
